title: Boos, anguish & fading belief - 'worrying day' for under-pressure Carrick
text:
For the second time in successive home Premier League games, Manchester United failed to beat opponents reduced to 10 men.

For the third time in as many seasons, a United manager finds himself under severe pressure before the clocks have gone back.

Four weeks ago, Manchester City needed an incorrect video assistant referee (VAR) decision to take advantage of an ineffective United performance after Phil Foden had been shown a red card in the 23rd minute for kicking out at Bruno Fernandes.

On Saturday, the damage was self-inflicted as a Spurs side, who had given every indication of being unable to score before Rodrigo Bentancur's headfirst charge at Luke Shaw just five minutes after Bryan Mbeumo's opener, came up with an injury-time equaliser.

Centre-back Lisandro Martinez was outmuscled embarrassingly easily by Dominic Solanke, with goalkeeper Senne Lammens failing to read the striker's deft touch that crept in at the far corner.

The anguish on United faces told its own story.

"A worrying day for Michael Carrick," observed former United skipper Gary Neville on Sky Sports.

Late Solanke strike salvages 10-man Spurs draw at Man Utd

Tottenham grab a draw but who got 1/10 - Ratings for Man Utd v Spurs

Manchester United have just six points from their opening six games of the Premier League season, their fewest at this stage of a league campaign since 1986-87, when they amassed four under Sir Alex Ferguson.

They have failed to win five of their six Premier League games this season (D3 L2), already as many as in 17 league games under Michael Carrick last season (W12 D3 L2).

United have collected two points from their last two games, both of which were against teams who began the match at the bottom of the Premier League.

In points terms they are closer to the relegation zone than the Champions League spots.

Carrick's side are now winless in four league games and face an always tricky trip across the Pennines to face old rivals Leeds at Elland Road on Sunday, 18 October. Either side of that are daunting Champions League trips to Atletico Madrid and Como.

United officials have repeatedly offered their backing to Carrick in recent weeks.

However, no fan needs reminding that two seasons ago a run of two wins in nine games in all competitions put Erik ten Hag under severe pressure before the axe fell after a defeat at West Ham on 27 October.

Last season, a combination of a shocking EFL Cup exit at the hands of League Two Grimsby and an insipid 3-1 loss at Brentford on 27 September did so much to undermine confidence in Ruben Amorim before he was sacked on 5 January.

The start to this campaign is starting to look increasingly familiar.

"I'm not happy with he amount of points we've got so far, for sure, you know," said Carrick.

"I'm not hiding, there's no hiding from that. I think it could have been different for a couple of little things here or there, but the reality is the reality, we've got to accept it, you know. We need to put things in a direction, in a positive direction quite quickly, that's pretty plain."

The 'little things' Carrick talks about are the defending for Solanke's goal, the lack of pressure put on Everton's Ainsley Maitland-Niles when he smashed another injury-time equaliser at the Hill Dickinson Stadium on 6 September, and the preventable Martinez own goal that nearly gave Fulham victory at Craven Cottage just before the international break.

"We've got to be a little bit more streetwise in moments, a little bit more stubborn and a little bit stronger in seeing out certain things," he added.

"It doesn't change my belief or the confidence in the players, you know. We're a really good team and capable of being a really good team, but we've obviously got to start getting more points on the board, that's for sure."

The problem is with each disappointment, the belief of United being 'a really good team' starts to ebb away.

Yet again, a post-match focus centred on how much Carrick's team ran, even though running for the sake of it has proved to be of little benefit.

"The stats don't lie when every time the other team runs more than you," said Sky Sports pundit and former Spurs captain Jamie Redknapp.

"Tottenham ran 5km more than Man United. OK, they had 10 men but that is every game. If you outrun your opposing number, you will win games. I'm not saying they are not trying. It is that physical battle they are losing though."

While, ex-Spurs midfielder Danny Murphy, added on BBC Match of the Day: "There was a lethargy about Man Utd, this midfield can't control games. It is partly tactical and partly personnel.

"I don't understand it. We saw at the end of last season Man Utd were much more organised and much more difficult to play against.

"The space in midfield was incredible and if they were playing against a more competent side, they would have been beaten. Play like that against good teams and they will be cut wide open."

It feels as though some fans are losing faith already, judging by the way they reacted at moments during the game, aside from the boos that accompanied the end of each half.

Forward Matheus Cunha - one of a number of Carrick's squad who have failed to reproduce the form he showed in the second half of last season - gestured to the crowd during the opening period. It wasn't clear whether he was responding to a negative comment or urging more noise, but the Brazilian clearly wasn't happy.

Carrick's family are season ticket holders. He knows what it is like to watch United struggle at Old Trafford.

"Obviously, it hurts," he said. "It hurts a lot. It's not nice to go through. I care as much as anybody about this place. Sometimes you could say too much because then it overspills. But it's coming from a good place, really, and so I understand it."

It is in moments like this that Carrick, who presents such a calm front in public, must be churning inside.…

title: Manchester United and Spurs come back to reality as City saga offers brief distraction | John Brewin
author: John Brewin at Old Trafford
text:
Manchester City’s rule breaches have dominated headlines and shifted focus from both clubs’ self-inflicted wounds

Turning back the clock is impossible. Up in the Stretford End’s middle tier, the ticker had returned, a retouching job to “51 years” invoiced for the pertinent sum of £114. The Manchester City that existed before the Abu Dhabi project won their last trophy in 1976. Questionable maths is perhaps not confined to the Etihad’s accounts department, though Manchester United’s support must get their kicks where they can.

Should City’s fall from grace be fully confirmed by the appeals and sanctions process , there is nothing in the way of irrefutable evidence of United’s former supremacy being restored. How United fans would love to return to 2008, when Michael Carrick was a key cog in Sir Alex Ferguson’s team of European champions. Instead, the autumn of 2026 brings a familiar swell of doubt, another manager dragged towards the meat grinder. It will be 40 years next month since Ferguson was appointed. A draw made United’s start to their league campaign the worst since then. The Carrick bounce has come to a standstill.

Sweet succour for City fans caught in legal limbo while railing against a “red cartel”. Should such a thing exist, United are a poor relation. Only Ipswich have been defeated by United this season in the Premier League, the latest disappointment to follow many years of corners being turned, only for culs-de-sac to be found. As the club who previously had the financial muscle to match the disguised funding of City, United have become the model for frittering away financial advantages. That the Glazer debt repayments since 2005 are a sum higher than City’s £900m-plus injection of petrodollars represents bitter irony. The cash has been flushed down a hole as deep as the Ship canal. That won’t be coming back either.

It can be readily argued that Tottenham have been more disadvantaged by City’s breaches. As with United, their lawyers have laid a legal marker against City for the compensation that could follow the completion of the Premier League process. Champions League revenue, extra Premier League prize money and attendant endorsements would have been helpful for a club that built a new stadium during those disputed years.

As with United, Tottenham’s self-inflicted wounds have been heavy. Whatever happens to the pariahs in blue, neither club can act as if the last 18 years were all a nasty dream. The City saga has been a welcome distraction when the international break might otherwise have been flush with speculation over the latest crises. Over close to 100 minutes, both teams personified the wastage and chaos that has reigned in north London and Stretford. A ragged affair, usually shapeless, full of errors forced and unforced, eventually boiled over. Rodrigo Bentancur was sent off, with Luke Shaw fortunate not to accompany the Uruguayan on a walk of shame. Both the goals scored owed much to defensive losses of concentration.

If Tottenham still lack a first Premier League win, they had their successes, and soon quietened the home support. Instead of rejoicing in City’s downfall with a flourish of vindication, as against Hull, as in the second half against Brighton, and three weeks ago, as against Fulham, United players were second to challenges, sluggish, space left achingly open.

Howls of anguish followed a chance that should have been buried by Mohammed Kudus. Further Tottenham chances followed. Boos accompanied Senne Lammens clearing his lines by belting the ball into the stands. Had Tottenham possessed anything like nerve in front of goal, they could have been beyond reach within an opening half hour that reduced Old Trafford to an anguished hush. Instead, the familiar path of beginning brightly to little avail was followed. If Spurs can start scoring goals they might be seriously dangerous. And yet they lie third-bottom of a Premier League table awaiting asterisks and appendices.

As prescribed by Roberto De Zerbi, Spurs counter-pressed with vigour, taking control of a midfield area where their opponents’ energy deficit was glaring. Carlos Baleba, signed for £70m, one of De Zerbi’s players at Brighton, arrived on the hour. The answer to a problem unsolved since Carrick’s retirement does not appear to be Youri Tielemans, who the debutant replaced. The Belgian, with significant miles on the clock, appears the latest example of United falling foul of buying cheap and probably needing to buy twice.

A marked increase in output that followed Baleba’s arrival pushed the game into United’s hands as Tottenham dropped off. De Zerbi-ball heavies the legs, particularly when rewards are scarce. Injustice, Bentancur’s red card, replenished them. Dominic Solanke’s goal, via unconventional means, came when the 10 men pushed onwards as United failed to press home their advantage, a pattern all too familiar this season. The anti-City chants were brought to a halt. Wallowing in others’ plight is little comfort when you are yourself stuck in the mud.

title: Carrick ‘massively disappointed’ after United drop points against 10-man Spurs
author: Jamie Jackson at Old Trafford
text:
Six points from six games is worst start since 1986

De Zerbi praises Spurs’ character after late equaliser

Michael Carrick was left “massively disappointed” by Manchester United’s 1-1 draw with Tottenham at Old Trafford and admitted they need more points after managing six from their opening six league games.

This is United’s poorest start to the season since 1986, Saturday’s draw coming when conceding Dominic Solanke’s added-time equaliser for 10-man Spurs, following Rodrigo Bentancur’s 78th-minute red card. The midfielder was sent off five minutes after Bryan Mbeumo’s opener had left United heading for only a second league victory.

Carrick said: “I am massively disappointed with the result, for sure. A mixed performance. I’m not happy with the amount of points that we’ve had so far. There’s no hiding from that. I think it could have been different for a couple of little things here or there, but the reality is the reality, we’ve got to accept it, you know. We need to put things in a direction, in a positive direction quite quickly, that’s pretty plain.”

United were disjointed throughout. The manager was asked if he felt let down by the players. “I don’t feel let down, because you can make mistakes. You can make mistakes, things go against you,” said Carrick. “I’ve made mistakes in games, and it’s not so much letting everyone down. We’ve all got standards, we’ve all got levels, the players have got levels and standards, and they hold their hands up at times when something goes against them.”

United’s fans jeered at times during the game. “When things aren’t quite going to plan, I understand the reaction at times,” said the manager. “Obviously, it hurts a lot. It’s not nice to go through, but sometimes you have to go through it, that’s how it is.

“I care as much as anybody about this place, so sometimes you could say too much because then it overspills. But it’s coming from a good place, really, and so I understand it.”

Bentancur might have caused a serious injury had a scissors-challenge on Shaw connected. Roberto De Zerbi backed his midfielder, who was sent off for a head-butt in the resulting melee.

“I kiss Rodrigo and say thanks,” said the Spurs manager. “It is clear it is a mistake from Rodrigo, it is not the right reaction in football but in that moment maybe with 10 players we played with more courage, more energy and for a long time Tottenham played without this blood this character. I am the coach and I want to see this character every game.”

While Spurs have only three points and remain winless, they are now off the bottom though remain in the relegation zone. “Today has been the game where for the first time this season we showed we are a team, we played for the teammates, we played together,” said De Zerbi.

author: Scott Murray
text: Two teams here who had some forward momentum going into the season with genuine hope of picking up speed; two teams who stalled on the starting line as the leading riders whistled off into the distance. Now then, it’s way too early to be bandying about talk of crisis … but Tottenham Hotspur are bottom of the table after being schooled at home by Aston Villa , while Manchester United required a late equaliser at no-win Fulham to ensure the three-week international hiatus wasn’t as much as a drag for their fans as it would have been without that verdict. Problem is, another unsatisfactory result isn’t going to help the off-stage mood music for any of these lads. So this is important. On offer tonight: a big momentum-shifter for both sides. Throw in the fact that this is one of the glamour fixtures in English football, and a cold start to the campaign can’t compromise the genuine sizzle when these two get together. The spark is lit at 5.30pm BST. It’s on!

title: Growing frustration at Old Trafford - analysis
text:
Manchester United entered the international window with just two wins from seven matches, with those coming against newly promoted Ipswich Town and Champions League debutants Sabah.

After disappointing home defeats to Manchester City and Brighton before the three-week break, the hosts had a point to prove to their disgruntled supporters.

But the fans were left unimpressed again by a lethargic first-half performance, with their players appearing to lack energy as the visitors pressed high and dominated.

Mohammed Kudus swept a strike just wide and Conor Gallagher had a close-range attempt smothered by Senne Lammens, who came to United's rescue again after the restart when got a hand to Solanke's sliding effort.

They were handed another lifeline through Mbeumo's goal, but could not capitalise on that, nor Rodrigo Bentancur's dismissal as Lammens was left rooted to the spot as Solanke got in front of Lisandro Martinez to head in the leveller.

Boss Michael Carrick's position may not be under immediate threat, despite United's worst start after four games since the 1986-87 campaign, but the frustration vented by the home fans at full-time indicate there is growing concern over the team's mentality.

It won't help Carrick's case that this was the second successive league game they have dropped points against a team that were reduced to 10 men - following their 1-0 derby defeat by Manchester City last month.

title: Solanke strikes late as 10-man Spurs salvage point at Manchester United
author: Jamie Jackson at Old Trafford
text:
After 72 laboured minutes, this match was lit up by a moment of quality. Matheus Cunha was fed by Luke Shaw down the left and the Brazilian crossed to Bryan Mbeumo, who spun and finished for Manchester United .

It drew delirious chants of “you’re going down with the City” with Spurs, at that stage, rock bottom of the Premier League and Manchester City’s long-term future in the division in question .

Uglier scenes followed for Spurs when Shaw chased Bruno Fernandes ball, leading Rodrigo Bentancur to launch an ugly scissor challenge that, if it had connected with the left-back, might have caused serious injury.

An incensed Shaw, surely reminded of his horrific double-leg break sustained 11 years ago at PSV, hared after Bentancur and shoved him over. Up came the midfielder to push his head into Shaw’s, who went down as a melee ensued.

Stuart Attwell sent Bentancur off and the referee issued yellow cards to Shaw – lucky to escape a red, too, for the push – and Jan Paul van Hecke.

All of this followed what had been a near snoozefest in which Spurs could not finish and United were disjointed: the tale, in microcosm, of their seasons.

There was more, though, as Tottenham registered an added-time equaliser and only their third league goal this season. Senne Lammens and Lisandro Martínez were United’s culprits as Sandro Tonali’s floated cross from the left should have been cleared by the Argentine but, instead, Dominic Solanke out-fought him and headed past Lammens, who watched it go in.

While averting a fourth defeat, Spurs still remain winless after their opening six league games for only a fourth time. This draw means there is no clear answer to the pre-game question of which manager is under more pressure, as both Roberto De Zerbi and Michael Carrick remain in need of a victory.

When the Italian scans the table, he will see his beleaguered side off the bottom but still in the relegation zone, while Carrick’s United remain in 12th and with a solitary victory.

De Zerbi now takes his squad to Marbella for warm-weather training, while Carrick’s men are at Atlético Madrid on Tuesday in the Champions League. They both need to conjure something.

After volleys of “you cheating bastards, you know what you are” rang out from both sets of fans, Lammens struggled with a nightmare start. A loose pass was intercepted by Lucas Bergvall and the ball rolled into Solanke. Yet, as has been Spurs’ problem, the centre-forward failed to finish, his shot saved by a relieved Lammens, who was jittery again when Martínez passed to him on his goalline, where he dawdled before hoofing clear.

The reports had stated how De Zerbi’s men have played well, at times this season, but cannot finish: a hindrance in this sport. No boon, too, for any team is hesitation, as when Youri Tielemans waited for the ball to bounce, Tottenham pounced, and suddenly Sávio was heading forward, the sliding challenge of Leny Yoro, fielded today at right back, saving a scattered rearguard.

This pointed to a Spurs ascendancy that was a headscratcher for Carrick and yet more Spurs profligacy saved United when Mohammed Kudus’s cross found Archie Gray and the young right-back beat Lammens but not his right post.

Carrick wants his team to control contests but there was close to zero control throughout. On the hour Carlos Baleba entered for his debut and immediately spun and flicked deftly into Fernandes’ path and you were reminded what skill can do.

Now came the breathless denouement – a point, at the close, feeling about fair.

title: Verstappen building major momentum as 'no-one very happy' at McLaren
text:
Max Verstappen is too far behind, and Kimi Antonelli too far ahead, to consider that Red Bull's revival might create any real jeopardy in the championship fight - but the Dutchman is certainly building some major momentum as the Formula 1 season moves into its closing stages.

Verstappen finished Saturday in Singapore with pole position for the grand prix to add to the sprint-race victory he had completed in tricky wet conditions earlier in the day.

And that gives him a great opportunity to complete a second grand prix victory within a week if he can convert on Sunday.

Verstappen has two eager Ferrari drivers right behind him, after Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton both felt that they had just missed out on a pole position that was possible.

He also has concerns about Red Bull's inconsistent starts - he lost the lead off the line both in Malaysia last weekend and in the sprint.

If he does drop back at the start in Singapore, it is the sort of track where overtaking is at a premium and he will not find it as easy to get back in front as he did on his way to his first victory of the season.

And he is, as one would expect, not getting ahead of himself.

"It was a good qualifying," Verstappen said. "It was always very close and we got ahead when it mattered and we are very happy with that.

"All weekend the car has been in a good window and that makes it a lot easier to find your rhythm. Incredibly happy to start first. Still a long race ahead, a lot of things can go wrong but we have done everything up until now well so hopefully we can continue that tomorrow.

"It's been a really positive last few races and we want to keep that momentum going."

Verstappen beats Ferraris to Singapore pole

Verstappen wins sprint after Russell crashes out

Verstappen's maiden win of the season at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia last weekend came after a run of three podium finishes in Italy, Spain and Azerbaijan, the last of which might very well have been a first victory had he not had problems in qualifying that left him eighth on the grid when he could have been on the front row.

His upturn in form has come as a result of steady work from Red Bull in improving their car and getting it into a position where he feels he can predict its behaviour and therefore push to the limit.

When a Red Bull is in that spot, Verstappen can be close to unbeatable.

He proved that in his remarkable comeback last year, when he gave McLaren and Lando Norris nightmares with a quite brilliant second half of the season that saw him eat into a 100-point deficit to the championship lead and ultimately miss out on taking a fifth title by just two points.

This year, Verstappen's deficit to Antonelli is even bigger than that.

He is 129 points behind the Mercedes driver with only 175 still remaining, assuming the two end-of-season races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi do actually take place in the context of the war in the Middle East.

It would take some kind of miracle - involving not only a non-stop stream of wins for Verstappen and a highly unlikely run of poor form and bad luck for Antonelli - for him to turn that around. So the prospect can be realistically dismissed.

But he certainly looks as if he will be a contender at the front for the remainder of the season.

If that is not a major concern for Antonelli, it certainly is for McLaren.

They had their own purple patch in the summer, when Lando Norris took consecutive wins in Hungary and the Netherlands, and would have won in Madrid had it not been for the unfortunate timing of a virtual safety car.

But the world champions have slipped from competitiveness in recent races, and before the Singapore Grand Prix they lie in third place in the constructors' championship, only 11 points ahead of Red Bull.

Saturday in Singapore was a bad day at the office for McLaren.

Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris were heading for fourth and fifth places in the sprint when Norris made a dive down the inside of his team-mate at Turn Five on the final lap.

This is not a common overtaking spot and from a McLaren point of view it was a move with no reward, only risk.

The move might have made sense if it had come earlier in the race and enabled Norris to challenge Leclerc, struggling in front of them, for third.

But on the last lap, Norris was not going to have a go at Leclerc even if he had got through - the only remaining overtaking place was at the end of the following straight into Turn Seven.

If the McLaren drivers swapped places, it would make no difference to the team in terms of a collective points haul, but if it went wrong, the cost could be high.

And so it did. Norris was in a position to make a legitimate move, but they came together, pirouetted in tandem, Piastri into the barriers and out of the race and Norris slipping down to eighth. Nine points had become one.

The stewards took no action, feeling that "both drivers had contributed to the incident".

Piastri had explained in the hearing that he did not expect Norris to try a move there, and attempted to leave space when he saw him.

Norris argued that his his car was in a position that, according to the rules, entitled him to make an overtaking attempt, so expected to be left space and had braked and gone over the kerb when he realised he was not going to get as much as he expected.

He said: "There are two sides, one is what the stewards say and that's a fair reasoning, no-one's to blame. But I did apologise because it was still me attacking, as I had the right to do. If I just sat there and was boring like I should be, nothing would have happened. So really it's still my fault but I deserved to go for the space and I still believe I had the right for it."

Norris added: "As you probably expect, no-one's very happy. I'm not happy, Oscar isn't happy. None of us wanted it to go that way. There was things both of us could have done better and, yeah, we spoke about it and we moved on."…

title: Russell bemoans "very bad" Saturday at Singapore GP
Verstappen beats Ferraris to Singapore pole
text:
Red Bull's Max Verstappen took his second pole position in a week by beating the Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton in qualifying at the Singapore Grand Prix.

Verstappen's first lap in final qualifying was enough to take pole, his time fending off a second lap from Leclerc that was 0.054 seconds off pole.

Hamilton was closest to Verstappen after the first runs but was unable to improve on his second run.

In fact, most of the front runners struggled to improve on their second runs, as Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli took fourth on the grid, from McLaren's Lando Norris.

Antonelli's team-mate George Russell was sixth fastest but will drop to the back of the grid with a penalty for using too many engine parts.

McLaren's Oscar Piastri was the only driver in the top four teams other than Leclerc to improve on his second run but could do no better than qualify seventh.

Alpine's Pierre Gasly and the Racing Bulls of Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad completed the top 10.

Verstappen wins sprint after Russell crashes out

Verstappen came to Singapore fresh from his and Red Bull's first victory of the season at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia and he has continued where he left off.

The four-time champion has looked the man to beat all weekend, and took pole for the grand prix a few hours after winning the sprint, following Russell crashing out of the lead.

Verstappen said: "This was the one I really wanted. The car has been really strong all weekend.

"We have been on a really on a positive trend and it's really special to take the pole here."

Leclerc felt pole had been on the cards if he had not made a few small mistakes on his final lap.

He said: "Q1 and Q2 were really difficult. I had some weird struggles under braking. Q3, the lap was OK. I did some mistakes. I think there was a potential to be on pole today but Max just did a better job."

Hamilton, second to Verstappen in the sprint, was quickest in the first and second parts of qualifying but could not repeat that pace when it mattered during what he described as "another difficult Q3".

He added: "The car was feeling much better. I really felt she had more in her, pushing her through the laps and sessions. Q1 and Q2 were awesome, but got to Q3, snaps through (Turns) One and Three (on the first lap) put me down and rest of the lap was good, and then the second lap too many snaps.

"I think there's a really fine line with our car whether you are over or under the sweet spot and I didn't get it quite right today."

title: Verstappen wins sprint after Russell crashes out
text:
Red Bull's Max Verstappen won an incident-packed sprint race at the Singapore Grand Prix after Mercedes driver George Russell crashed out of the lead.

Russell was leading in tricky conditions, with half the track dry and half wet, when he got a little too wide at the final corner at the end of the first lap.

He lost control of his Mercedes, which spun across the track into the inside wall, before bouncing back again to the outside, the rest of the field somehow avoiding him.

Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton took second having made a superb start from sixth on the grid with team-mate Charles Leclerc third.

A final-lap collision between the McLarens as Lando Norris tried to pass Oscar Piastri at Turn Five promoted Russell's team-mate Kimi Antonelli to fourth place.

In combination with Russell's retirement, that extends the Italian's championship lead to 89 points.

A chaotic race saw the start delayed by 30 minutes by a tropical downpour, and then Verstappen navigating a safety car period following Russell's accident, a restart, and initial pressure from Hamilton to eventually ease away into a comfortable lead.

It was the Dutchman's second Formula 1 win in seven days, after his maiden victory this season at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, and the first time he has won in Singapore.

The rain before the start hit only parts of the track. The second sector stayed dry while the first sector, particularly Turns Two and Three, were soaking wet with standing water.

Once the rain abated, the field did two laps behind a safety car to check conditions before racing began with a standing start.

Russell gave himself a golden opportunity to breathe some life into his almost-extinguished title hopes when he beat Verstappen off the line and took the lead into the first corner.

But after leading the first lap, he made a mistake at the final corner.

Russell said: "I just misjudged it, got more power than I was expecting from the battery, got a little wider than I expected and touched the white line. Rule number one in the wet is don't touch the white line. Very silly mistake."

That left Verstappen in front, with Hamilton behind. But after the seven-time champion pursued his erstwhile 2021 title rival for a few laps, the Red Bull began to ease away and was clearly in control, leading Hamilton, Leclerc, Piastri, Norris and Antonelli.

With overtaking difficult around Marina Bay, the field was static until the closing stages.

Leclerc was struggling, and he began to be caught by the McLarens and Antonelli.

Norris had been pressuring Piastri for some laps before the Australian also began to close in on Leclerc, and Antonelli, struggling with oversteer in the early laps, picked up the pace.

On the final lap, Norris made a better exit out of Turn Three and saw an opportunity to try to pass Piastri at Turn Five, but Piastri defended his position robustly, the cars touched, and spun in unison.

Norris was initially far enough alongside to make a legitimate passing attempt, but having apparently tried to back out of the move, not so at the apex to satisfy the driving standards rules.

But the criticism of Norris will be that he miscalculated the risk-reward, that it was an ill-advised, marginal move against his team-mate for little gain - a point was at stake - and none for the team, as it would have not changed their collective points total.

The stewards investigated the incident but took no action on the basis that both drivers had contributed to the incident.

Piastri, who hit the barriers, was out on the spot, but Norris was able to keep going, although he fell down to eighth, behind Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson, Haas driver Oliver Bearman and Audi's Nico Hulkenberg.

title: Premier League today: How to watch Manchester United v Spurs, TV channels & live stream
author: Graham Ruthven
text:
How will Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options

The sense of desperation will be strong as Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur arrive at Old Trafford with both teams in bad need of a win to change the narrative around their disappointing seasons so far.

Anything less than three points would further increase the pressure on Michael Carrick and Roberto De Zerbi , both of whom are fighting to prove they are the right people for their respective jobs. Saturday’s match could be pivotal.

Spurs can take encouragement from the fact they have won four of their last six encounters with United in all competitions dating back to September 2024. Less positive is their run of four blanks in the five league matches they have played so far this season.

Here is your complete guide on how to watch today’s Premier League fixture, including kick-off times, broadcast networks, and online streaming options.

United Kingdom: Watch on Sky Sports Main Event

Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur have suffered many of the same problems to start the season. Both teams have conceded far too many goals and struggled for any sort of defensive foundation. The former have yet to keep a single clean sheet in five league games while the latter have kept just two.

In midfield, Carrick and De Zerbi struggling for the right balance. Manchester United and Spurs both bought expensive new midfielders in the summer transfer window who have yet to settle into their new surroundings.

Things haven’t been much better in the attacking third where Spurs have scored in just one of their five league games. For Manchester United, the likes of Marcus Rashford, Benjamin Sesko and Bryan Mbeumo have yet to find top form. This match could be a catalyst, but it’s not clear for whom.

Player to watch: Kobbie Mainoo, Manchester United – The 21-year-old has been United’s best player in the early part of the campaign and will be central to the home team gaining traction through the middle of the pitch. Mainoo could control the game.

The State Pension age went up again this week as part of its gradual shift from 66 years old to 67. The law says it will rise again to 68 by 2046, but that may change. A State Pension Age Review, the third to be held, is considering whether the rules around state pension age are appropriate in the light of the latest life expectancy data and will recommend how state pension age should be determined in the future. We'll speak to Dr Suzy Morrissey, who was appointed by the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions last year to prepare an independent report into the future of the State Pension age. Louise Botting, the former presenter of Money Box, has died at the age of 87 after a short illness. We'll pay tribute. Average mortgage rates hit a three year high this week affecting millions of homes owners looking to remortgage and people hoping to buy their first home. What's the best advice? And, the Bank of England has picked the animals to appear on the next series of bank notes. The hedgehog, barn owl, puffin and bumblebee were chosen after a public vote - with almost half a million people responding to a consultation.
